world.title: Six Somali Supreme Court Judges File Case at East African Court of Justice
world.description: ARUSHA, Six Somali Supreme Court judges have filed a case against the Federal Republic of Somalia at the East African Court of Justice, after the court’s First Instance Division issued a notification on November 18 giving the government 45 days to respond to a reference challenging the removal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed and the paralysis of the country’s highest judicial institution. The applicants include Justice Dr. Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, Justice Salah Sh. Ibrahim Diblaw, Justice Abdikadir Idiris Essa, Justice Dr. Abubakar Ahmed Ali, Justice Dr. Abdikafar Hussein Isak, and Justice Abdiaziz Mohamed Yusuf. The respondents are the State Attorney General and the Federal Republic of Somalia. The notification, issued under Rule 26 of the court’s procedures, requires the government to file a response within 45 days or face a default determination. The Constitutional Crisis Behind the Filing The case stems from a sequence of events that began on November 4, when President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud announced the dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. The dismissal came one day before the Supreme Court was expected to rule on a petition filed by former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed challenging constitutional amendments that extended the mandates of the president, parliament, and federal government, as FTL Somalia reported. On November 5, the Supreme Court’s five-member Constitutional Division ruled that the amendments could not be applied retroactively to sitting institutions. The court determined that President Mohamud’s four-year mandate expired on May 15, 2026, and that parliament’s mandate ended on April 14. It ordered political stakeholders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, according to FTL Somalia’s coverage of the ruling. science.title: Social norm strength varies between cultures with respect to norm referent, norm type, contextualization, normative properties, and valence
science.description: Leading theoretical accounts in cultural psychology argue that social norms are generally stronger in certain cultures across different types of norms. However, these theories have largely been based on studies focusing on a limited range of norms and specific measures, with little attention paid to which specific social norms are under consideration. To address this limitation, we assess social norms across a broader range of features, including norm referent (whether norms are for behaviors vs. emotions), norm type (prescriptive vs. descriptive), norm contextualization (context-specific vs. in general), norm assessment (homogeneity vs. concordances), and valence (for emotion norms: positive vs. negative). Two studies (total N = 3344) conducted in Japan, South Korea, the United States (Studies 1–2), and the United Kingdom (Study 2) reveal significant variation across all features. Furthermore, norms frequently vary more within cultural regions than between them, challenging the assumption of clear-cut cultural differences. These findings suggest that existing theories may have overstated cross-cultural differences in norm strength by having focused on a limited subset of norms, and highlight the need to consider which norms are assessed. As an alternative to the existing theories, and as a benchmark for future theoretical accounts, we propose a specificity principle for cultural differences in norm strength.

science.title: Mapping temperature using transmission Kikuchi diffraction
science.description: As electronic devices are engineered at increasingly smaller length scales, new nanoscopic metrologies are needed. Measuring nanoscale temperatures and pressures is challenging as physical contact inevitably perturbs the system, and collecting far-field thermal radiation limits the spatial resolution. Kikuchi diffraction thermometry (KDTh), a non-contact scanning electron microscope (SEM) technique, can sensitively map nanoscale temperatures. Local lattice changes measured by Kikuchi pattern fitting enable translating volumetric strain to temperature via the material’s coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). Measurements on Joule-heated graphite come from rastering a 5.5-nm electron probe across the sample, achieving a  ~ 0.01% fractional precision and 2.2 K/$$\sqrt{{{\rm{Hz}}}}$$ temperature sensitivity. KDTh offers superior sensitivity by fitting the entire Kikuchi pattern, instead of a particular Kikuchi band or interband angle. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques can achieve a similar precision, but electron-transparency limits their applications. KDTh can operate in both transmission and reflection modes to cost-effectively accommodate a variety of samples. Measuring nanoscale temperatures is hard: contact probes perturb samples and optical methods lack resolution. Here, authors develop Kikuchi diffraction thermometry, a non-contact electron microscopy method that maps nanoscale temperatures via tiny heat-induced lattice changes.
